title: Race and Strict Scrutiny
short: Racial classifications get strict scrutiny: Strauder v. West Virginia (1880) struck down excluding Black men from juries; Korematsu (1944) upheld the wartime exclusion order and has since been repudiated; Loving (1967) struck down interracial marriage bans.
trouble: Students think Korematsu applied rational basis. The Court said racial restrictions are "immediately suspect" and get "the most rigid scrutiny," and still upheld the order; it is now cited as a warning.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The Fourteenth Amendment was adopted in 1868 above all to protect the newly freed. Racial classifications are the first and clearest target of equal protection, and today they get strict scrutiny: the government must show a compelling interest and a law narrowly tailored to it.

opts.name: Strauder v. West Virginia
opts.q: May a state law allow only white men to serve on juries?
opts.holding: No; excluding Black men from juries by law violates equal protection.
opts.facts: West Virginia law allowed only white men to serve on juries. Taylor Strauder, a Black man, was convicted of murder by an all-white jury.
opts.reasoning: The Court said the amendment's purpose was to protect the formerly enslaved and their race from discriminatory laws, and that excluding Black men from juries by law marked them as inferior and denied the defendant equal protection.

opts.facts: During World War II, military orders excluded all people of Japanese ancestry, citizens and noncitizens, from parts of the West Coast. About 120,000 people were removed and most were held in camps. Fred Korematsu, a U.S. citizen, stayed in California and was convicted.
opts.reasoning: Justice Black wrote that legal restrictions on a single racial group are "immediately suspect" and must get "the most rigid scrutiny," but the Court deferred to military judgments about the risk of espionage and sabotage.
opts.dissent: Justices Roberts, Murphy and Jackson dissented. Murphy said the exclusion fell into "the ugly abyss of racism."
opts.later: In 1983 a federal court vacated Korematsu's conviction; Congress apologized and paid redress in the Civil Liberties Act of 1988. The Supreme Court has since said Korematsu was wrongly decided.

blocks.html: Korematsu is a strange landmark. It announced the language of strict scrutiny and then failed to apply it with any rigor. Today it is cited as a warning about deference in a crisis. Strict scrutiny now means what it says: in the Court's words, racial classifications are justified only by the most compelling reasons, and the means must fit them closely. Loving v. Virginia (1967) applied this to Virginia's ban on interracial marriage, rejecting the state's argument that the law was valid because it punished both races equally; Adarand Constructors, Inc. v. Peña (1995) held that federal racial classifications get the same scrutiny.

events.label: Civil Liberties Act: apology and redress

blocks.html: Racial classifications get strict scrutiny: a compelling interest and narrow tailoring, with the burden on the government. Strauder v. West Virginia (1880) struck down all-white juries by law; Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld the exclusion order while calling race "immediately suspect"; Congress apologized in 1988, and the Supreme Court has since said Korematsu was wrongly decided.

blocks.title: Equal application
blocks.q: A state says its law forbidding marriage across racial lines is valid because it applies to all races equally. Under Loving, does that save it?
steps: The law still classifies by race: whether you may marry depends on the race of both people.
Loving rejected "equal application" as a defense and applied strict scrutiny.
The only purpose was to maintain white supremacy, which is not a legitimate interest at all.
blocks.a: No; equal application does not avoid strict scrutiny.

blocks.title: Korematsu's test
blocks.q: Which standard did the Korematsu majority say applied, and what did the Court decide?
steps: The majority said racial restrictions are "immediately suspect" and get "the most rigid scrutiny."
It nonetheless upheld the exclusion order, deferring to military judgment.
blocks.a: The most rigid scrutiny in words; the order was upheld.

blocks.html: Thinking Korematsu applied rational basis. The Court said racial restrictions are "immediately suspect" and get "the most rigid scrutiny," and still upheld the order. Its fault was deference, not the stated test. Check: the case is now cited as a warning, and the Supreme Court has since said it was wrongly decided.
